newsitem.title: GERMANY: German union readies protests on wage talk reform.
newsitem.headline: German union readies protests on wage talk reform.

text.p: IG Metall, Germany's largest and most militant trade union, warned on Thursday it would react with strong protest action to any government move to alter laws on Germany's free collective wage bargaining system.

The threat came after it emerged that a discussion paper had been drawn up by a senior government politician proposing to relax the rules of a bargaining system that has become a sacred cow to post-war German trade unionists.
"If the government attacks the free bargaining system, it risks a conflict that will make the sick pay dispute look modest," IG Metall deputy chairman Walter Riester said in a statement.

Riester was referring to the protests and walkouts involving hundreds of thousands of workers last year which eventually led to many companies deciding not to implement a new law allowing them to reduce sick pay entitlements.

A spokeswoman at IG Metall's headquarters in Frankfurt, while denying a media report that it was planning all-out strikes, said "a range of action from demonstrations onwards" was foreseeable if the government went ahead with the changes.

At issue is a paper drafted by Hans-Peter Repnik, deputy leader of the parliamentary faction of Chancellor Kohl's Christian Democrats, which proposes making existing wage bargaining laws more open to interpretation.
Currently, German labour law favours a bargaining system under which unions and management umbrella groups negotiate work agreements that apply across a specified industry sector.

Thus, the 1997-98 wage increases agreed in the metal and engineering sector late last year should in theory apply across the board from industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG to a 20-employee tool-making business.

But an increasing number of particularly small and medium firms are saying that tougher business conditions mean they now need company-specific clauses that would, for example, allow them to reduce working hours during business slumps.
Unions have in the past always resisted attempts by employers to break away from sector-wide agreements.

Germany's Trade Union Federation (DGB) body has now responded by saying that it is ready to discuss ways to make sector-wide wage contracts more like guidelines on which individual firms can base their own wage deals.
It said it would be meeting employer groups in late February to discuss issues including the continued application of sector-wide wage agreements.

IG Metall, however, whose chairman Klaus Zwickel feels betrayed by the collapse of a government-sponsored job creation initiative last year, believes that free collective bargaining must continue to be honoured as a principle.

The threat of protest action comes as the union also plans demonstrations against tax reform proposals detailed last week under which bonuses for weekend, night and public holiday shifts would in future be taxed.

An IG Metall spokeswoman in North Rhine-Westphalia, the steel-making region where the union counts its highest membership, said it was already in contact with factory work councils there over possible industrial action.
